citations.narrative:
An enclosure housing two black and white ruffed lemurs contains a door in need of repair. The door has been secured
shut and serves as part of the lemur enclosure wall. Across this door is a small kitchen area used for preparing the bird
diets. Facing into the lemur enclosure, localized at the bottom center of the door is a hole approximately 2.5 inches in
length and 1.5 inches in height. The licensee indicated that wires used to traverse this hole and were removed once the
area was made into a lemur enclosure, but the hole was never closed. Extending the length of the bottom of the door, in a
water mark appearance, is deteriorating wood. The outer surface of the door is raised and irregularly textured due to the
expansion of the wood beneath it. At the bottom left corner, the surface of the door has worn off resulting in the beginning
of a second hole. When the door is viewed from the outside of the enclosure, its surface is similar in appearance
indicating the whole thickness of the bottom of the door is affected and decaying.
The door is in need of repair. Failure to replace this door will perpetuate its decay and affect the structural stability of the
wall of the enclosure. The housing facilities for nonhuman primates must be designed and constructed so that they are
structurally sound and must be kept in good repair.
Correct by 10/30/2026

Bird feed is not being stored in a manner that protects the feed from contamination and vermin infestation. The facility is
storing bags of feed in tin containers with lids, though some are not securely attached resulting in the entry of pests. One
container stored an open bag of Mazuri mini bird feed with several live grain weevils contained within it. When the
inspector asked the facility representative to pick up the bag of feed, live weevils were seen crawling at the bottom of the
container as well as beneath the bag. A second tin container was opened and no bugs were observed inside the bag of
parrot and macaw feed labeled Goldenfeast Madagascar blend. Though, beneath the bags live weevils were observed
crawling around them. Located next to the weevils were remnants of small, oval, dark brown, cockroach egg capsules as
well as mealworms that were not part of the open bag of bird feed. Additionally, the area being used to store the feed felt
warm and damp to the inspector indicating a potential increase in moisture and a suitable environment for grain weevil
development.
The presence of several live grain weevils can reduce the nutritional value and overall quality of the bird feed. If not
controlled a heavy infestation can result in the development of fungus and mold which can be harmful to birds. Please
correct by ensuring the food is stored in a manner that protects the supplies from deterioration spoilage, contamination,
and vermin infestation.
Correct by this day forward.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representatives.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
Deputy Administrator
APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
